title: Book XI
frozenSupport: Book XI opens by describing the rational soul as self-seeing, self-analyzing, self-shaping, and complete wherever life stops it.
Marcus reduces song, dancing, tragedy, comedy, and spectacle by dividing them into parts so they lose power over judgment.
The chapter insists the present condition is fit for philosophy and uses the branch image to describe hatred, separation, and regrowth into the social whole.
Justice is treated as the foundation of the virtues, and Marcus pairs steady action with gentleness and benevolence toward those who hinder him.
Later sections emphasize the spherical soul, present-life focus, contempt for praise and hatred, and the rule: if it is not right, do not do it; if it is not true, do not say it.
allowedClaims: the rational soul can make each act complete even under interruption
dividing spectacle into parts weakens fascination without erasing all value
social separation is a self-cutting that can still be repaired
justice and benevolence must remain united under obstruction
truthful speech and right action are part of one rational discipline
doNotClaim: that Marcus rejects all art or performance as worthless by definition
that benevolence means yielding to injustice
that calm alone is sufficient without truth and justice
